questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Ireland was always my dream destination to do my exchange and to me it was crucial that it was an English speaking country so that I could focus on my studies and improve my academic English. It was also important to me that I chose a country which was not too far from Denmark – so I would have an easy opportunity to go back and visit afterwards. Furthermore, I had only heard good things about Ireland as a country and the Irish people

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had the most wonderful time during my exchange semester and would highly recommend it to anyone considering it. Ireland and Trinity College Dublin was a great choice of destination and besides gaining new friends and experiences, I also gained new knowledge, language skills and perspectives

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Orientation happened online and while I acknowledge the difficult times we've been though, I would have wished it was in person. The orientation consisted of a few zoom presentations about the university, living in Dublin and IT. I never got the chance to meet the other exchange students or officially tour the campus before I started classes. That said, the orientation covered most of my questions and the ones I had afterwards were answered quickly

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I didn't need much assistance upon my arrival. Only small things related to my university e-mail account, student travel card and other miscellaneous stuff. Everything else related to my stay I figured out on my own without involving Trinity

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Trinity has lots of societies and while I was introduced to a few during orientation, most of them I had to look up or research myself. It would have been nice if an introduction to the societies were part of the general orientation, but I assume that that's just part of doing the exchange during the second semester. I found it easy to get my questions answered before my arrival to Dublin. I had a contact person within the law school in Trinity and she was easy to reach and answered my questions quickly, e.g. regarding course registration and orientation

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was fairly easy to find housing. I started searching in October (and left for my exchange in January) and had quite a few options. I never considered finding housing through Trinity as I had read from previous experiences that it was difficult. I ended up living in a student accommodation – consisting of a flat with individual rooms and a kitchen shared between 6 people. It was great and although expensive, I was  happy with my choice of accommodation as it gave an instant network and people to come home to after class/activities

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Housing in Dublin is expensive. Much more than in Denmark. Most of my budget went towards rent, but I also chose a housing option where everything was paid and I didn't have to worry about bills or touring the place beforehand. Make up your mind about your priorities – Is it important to live close to campus? Does it have to be the cheapest option? Do you want flatmates? Start looking for a place to live as soon as possible. I had a few friends who were left with very expensive or far away options because they started searching too late

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Be prepared to pay a high rent and maybe research a bit about the neighbourhoods in Dublin. The city is small enough that everything is reachable by foot, but maybe you have preferences regarding food and pub options, nature or transport

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I didn't register for my classes until a week before they were supposed to start. To me it was kind of a stress factor, but I was in contact with the university beforehand and they assured me that it was meant to happen that late. You'll get an overview of the different classes/modules Trinity offers to visiting students including the exam form and who they are taught by. This can also be found on Trinity's website

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I registered via a Google Docs that was send to me by my Erasmus coordinator after having received a time table that showed the different classes and when they were taught. We weren't allowed to take clashing classes. The different times weren't available until the week before, so make sure you get more classes preapproved than you need – that way you'll have options if your preferred classes clash

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I had an Erasmus coordinator at the law school in Trinity who was easy to reach and helped with all my questions regarding classes, time tables and course registration

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very successful. I got the classes I had wished for and while the whole process happened much later than what I'm used to at UCPH, the process was also quite quick and efficient

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make sure you get more modules preapproved than you need. Just in case your chosen ones clash. Look at the exam form of each module. Trinity has a lot more exams consisting of essays, response papers or presentations compared to UCHP. It's a great way to try out something new and I quickly learned that if you have different exam forms, it's more likely that the exams are spread out throughout the semester instead of happening all at ones during one week. I had three modules and ended up having deadline dates/exam dates in March, mid-April, end of April and mid-May – very manageable

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was very satisfied. The academic programme at Trinity was quite different from what I was used to – but that was also what I wished for when I decided to go on exchange. First of all, the academic semester is much shorter than at UCPH. I started classes the last week of January and ended them in the beginning of April. I then had about three weeks before my first exam and then a week until the next one. So my academic semester was over in the beginning of May. However, it gave me a lot of opportunities to travel and discover Ireland. Secondly, all classes are 50-minutes each and you'll usually only have one at a time. And lastly, everything that you need to know is taught during the lectures. I only bought one book for the semester and only opened it a couple of times. That might have been the biggest difference from the academic programme at UCPH. However, overall I was very satisfied with the programme and getting to experience a different style of teaching in a different language

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: We only had a small selection of modules we could take as visiting students. I ended up choosing one 1st and 2nd year module and two 3rd and 4th year modules. There was definitely a difference between the levels of the two, but I was happy to experience both. I had the feeling that when you're visiting as a masters student, you'll always find the level a bit easier than what you are used to, but I guess that is made up for by the difference in teaching style and language

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The teaching style at Trinity was quite different from the one I was used to at UCPH. I had almost only lectures consisting of the professor making a presentation of the subject for 50 minutes. This was done in a big auditorium. Questions were very welcomed, but there was no group work or discussions involved. In one of my classes I had 4 seminars throughout the semester. These were 50-minute classes with only 12 people where we were given a set of questions beforehand and talked through them in class. They didn't provided a lot of new knowledge as most of the things were covered during the lectures, but it was a good diversion in the teaching style. As long as you're prepared that most teaching will happen as lectures you'll be fine and I honestly found it quite relaxing to have a semester where I mostly listened

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Conflict of Laws, Employment Law and Criminal Law

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I had such a great time taking Conflict of Laws. It was a very interesting and relevant class – especially if you have taken Civilproces at UCPH. The professor, David Kenny, was very smart, interesting and had a great approach to teaching. If you have an interest in employment law, then I would also highly recommend taking the Employment Law class. Criminal Law was a year 1 and 2 module, so everyone was quite young and new to law. However, it was quite interesting to get a look at the criminal law from an Irish and common law perspective

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: It wasn't unexpected, but housing took up most of my budget. Other than that I felt like I was fairly prepared for the costs

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Buying groceries were definitely less expensive than in Denmark. I only got one book for the semester (which ended up not being necessary), so that was also less expensive. Transportation became cheaper while I was there and with the Student Leap Card (travel card) you're able to get the bus or tram for only 1 €. Traveling around Ireland wasn't too expensive either, but I guess I ended up travelling a bit more than I had anticipated so that added up. In general I found that I was spending more during the last couple of months of my exchange – I went out more, travelled more, met friends for food or coffee more. Just a side note when making or preparing a budget

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Dublin and Trinity really has so much to offer and especially with everything being normal and in-person again. I was only affected by restrictions during the first couple of weeks of my stay and for most of the semester everything was open and normal. There are so many opportunities to learn, explore and experience. I also found the academic semester to be shorter and not as busy as what I'm used to at UCPH, so it was great to have a lot of things to do during my free time

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Trinity has a ton of different societies and sports clubs. There is something for everyone. I ended up signing up for the yoga society, the knitting society, the international students society and the hiking society. I didn't necessarily attend a lot of the events but the ones I did I really enjoyed. Go to the events/meet-ups as early as possible – everyone is new and this is the opportunity to meet new friends. I met a great group of other exchange students in the international students society on a hike during my first month and they ended up being some of my best friends. In general, the societies are a great way to meet a bunch of new people who don't necessarily study the same as you – something we could learn from at UCPH and in Denmark

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Join the societies and Erasmus-WhatsApp/Facebook groups – this is a great way to meet other students and visiting students to do all the fun things with. Maybe try and have a weekly thing that you do. I really wanted to take Irish language classes (but had trouble finding a place) and a few of my friends did dance classes or drawing classes. I also found Instagram (Dublin accounts) to be a great way of knowing what went on in the city and which places to go to

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Please, go and explore what Ireland has to offer. I loved Dublin and everything that the city has to offer, but Ireland is so much more. Try to do this throughout the semester. I saved most of my travels for May (where I didn't have classes), but wished that I had done many more weekend trips to the different cities and counties in Ireland. When staying in and around Dublin, go on daytrips to Howth (most beautiful place), Bray and Glendalough. Visit the parks and museums in Dublin (The little museum of Dublin is a must), go on walks, drink at all the pubs, visit some of the whiskey distilleries, go see plays and in general just have fun while you're there. Dublin is a fairly small city and everything is reachable within walking distance. Ireland really has so much to offer

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was very easy. The Irish culture is very like the Danish one. People like to have fun, go for a pint or coffee and just talk. However, Irish people are much more open towards visitors and tourists. I've only met kind people who were interested in my culture and talking/explaining about their own. Dublin also has a lot of non-Irish people living in the city so the culture is very diverse and you'll find almost every other country represented in the food available or small communities around the city

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: If you want to meet Irish students then my best tip would have to be to join the societies. Here you'll find both local and international students and you won't necessarily share the same studies, but you'll share the same interest whether that's hiking, knitting, dancing or planting flowers. Otherwise, go to a pub, get a pint and start talking to the people at the table next to you. I can almost guarantee it's gonna be the most interesting conversation of your life

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: If I had to pick something, it would probably be the approach to time. I'm very used being punctual about being somewhere at the right time and Irish people are a bit more relaxed when it comes to that. It wasn't a big problem though and as soon as you realise the difference you'll adapt quite quickly

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I learned to highly appreciate the pub culture. Even if you are not a big drinker, the pub isn't necessarily about going out for five pints each night and get drunk. It's a place people meet up like a café and have a pint and a great conversation. Dublin is booming with pubs, so try out a bunch a find the one you like. I also just really appreciated the friendly approach to new people and visitors. It's a very easy culture to be a foreigner in

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Start building a network as soon as possible. It can be daunting (at least it was for me), but it's so rewarding to have friends to talk to and do things with. So go to the pub, join the society and say yes whenever possible. Explore everything Dublin and Ireland has to offer. It's so easy (and fairly cheap) to travel around so make it a priority to be cultural and visit all the places around you. And lastly, I would recommend to take part in the Trinity culture. Go to the classes, join the societies, take part in the events that are happening and make use of all the facilities. It'll be over before you know it

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Do some research before arriving at Trinity. Find out what Trinity has to offer (events, student discounts, tours, language classes etc.) and make use of it. Also, Trinity has a lot of great places to study in and the campus is situated right in the centre of the city, so there are lots of great coffee places and cafes around to study in

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The most rewarding part was probably all the new people I met and befriended. Both Irish and international people. I now have great connections in a lot of different places. In general, I just found it very rewarding to now have a place so close by to call home. I really made it a priority to get to know Dublin very well and feel at home in the city and I feel like I succeeded with that

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I never really experienced any great challenges. The closest thing was being unsure of how to make friends when I first arrived. I chose to arrive a few weeks before classes started and I do remember being anxious about not meeting very many people. But as soon as classes and societies started, that problem solved itself fairly quickly. It was like a rolling snowball – once you meet a few people, you'll meet a bunch soon afterwards

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Going on exchange is such a unique opportunity. Do it because you want to want to know a new culture, make friends from around the world and have great experiences. Improving your academic studies and resume should be a factor in your decision, but not the only one. Make sure you go because you are curious about life and others. Go to Ireland. It has so much to offer and you'll be able to come back easily and relive the best semester of your life

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
